title: Day 51: Modbus Protocol Suite: Modbus RTU, RS-485 Serial & Modbus TCP Industrial Bridging
summary: Modbus is the universal protocol of industrial operational technology (OT), operating over RS-485 differential serial links (RTU) and Ethernet TCP/IP port 502 (TCP).
Modbus RTU framing relies on physical bus silence: a 3.5 character silent interval (t3.5) demarcates the beginning and end of binary frames.
Error detection in Modbus RTU is governed by a 16-bit CRC using reflected polynomial 0xA001, transmitted in little-endian byte order.
The Modbus data model defines four tables: Discrete Inputs (1x), Coils (0x), Input Registers (3x), and Holding Registers (4x), manipulated via standard function codes.
Modbus TCP replaces serial CRC-16 and t3.5 intervals with a 7-byte MBAP header, supporting client multiplexing and persistent TCP streaming.
goal: Master the Modbus industrial protocol suite: implement RS-485 framing and t3.5 silent interval detection, calculate Modbus CRC-16 with polynomial 0xA001, model slave register tables and function codes, construct Modbus TCP MBAP headers, and engineer a multi-unit industrial gateway bridge.

parts.title: Day 51 Part 1 — Modbus RTU Framing, RS-485 Physical Layer & 3.5 Character Silent Interval
say: Welcome to Day 51 and the beginning of Month 2 Block 11 of our advanced IoT curriculum: Industrial IoT (IIoT), SCADA Protocols & OT/IT Convergence. In this module, we transition from commercial wireless meshes and cellular protocols into the hardened world of industrial automation, factory floors, substations, and process plants. At the heart of industrial operational technology (OT) stands the Modbus protocol, developed by Modicon in 1979. Despite being over four decades old, Modbus remains the universal lingua franca of industrial field devices—connecting programmable logic controllers (PLCs), variable frequency drives (VFDs), digital power meters, and environmental sensors across millions of industrial plants worldwide.

Modbus RTU (Remote Terminal Unit) operates primarily over physical RS-485 balanced differential serial buses. Unlike single-ended RS-232, which is vulnerable to electromagnetic noise in noisy factory environments, RS-485 uses a twisted pair (Lines A and B) to transmit differential voltage signals. A logical '1' (mark) is represented by Line A being more negative than Line B ($V_A - V_B < -200\,\text{mV}$), while a logical '0' (space) is represented by Line A being more positive than Line B ($V_A - V_B > +200\,\text{mV}$). This differential signaling cancels out common-mode electromagnetic noise induced by nearby high-voltage motors, arc welders, and heavy machinery, enabling reliable multidrop communication across distances of up to 1200 meters (4000 feet) at baud rates ranging from 9600 bps to 115200 bps.

Because Modbus RTU is a compact binary protocol with no explicit packet start delimiters, frame synchronization is achieved entirely through timing: the 3.5 character silent interval ($t_{3.5}$). A message frame must begin and end with a silent interval of at least 3.5 character times on the physical bus. At 9600 baud with 11-bit characters (1 start bit, 8 data bits, no parity, 2 stop bits), a single character takes approximately 1.146 milliseconds; therefore, $t_{3.5}$ equals 4.01 milliseconds. The receiver's UART driver continuously monitors inter-character idle times. If an idle gap exceeding 1.5 character times ($t_{1.5}$) occurs during transmission, the incomplete frame is considered corrupt and discarded. Once a full $t_{3.5}$ idle duration is detected following a transmission, the receiving slave knows the frame is complete and initiates address decoding and CRC verification.

In our hands-on implementation, we construct the `ModbusRtuParser`. We calculate character transmission times and $t_{3.5}$ silent interval thresholds across various baud rates, enforce inter-frame idle validation, extract the slave address and function code, and verify complete frame demarcation.

To fully understand the physical robustness of Modbus RTU in harsh industrial environments, we must examine the electrical transmission dynamics of the TIA/EIA-485-A (RS-485) balanced differential standard. Unlike single-ended signaling schemes such as RS-232, where signal voltage is measured relative to a shared local chassis ground, RS-485 transmits data across two complementary conductors designated as Line A (inverting) and Line B (non-inverting). When transmitting a binary '0', the differential driver drives Line A higher than Line B; when transmitting a binary '1', Line B is driven higher than Line A. Because the two conductors are twisted tightly together along the cable run, any external electromagnetic interference (EMI)—such as high-voltage transients induced by nearby variable frequency drives (VFDs) or electrical switching gear—couples equally into both wires. At the receiver, an instrumentation differential amplifier measures only the difference between the two conductors ($V_A - V_B$), completely canceling out the induced common-mode noise.

Furthermore, proper physical bus termination and biasing are mandatory to prevent transmission line reflections and erratic framing errors. An RS-485 cable acts as a transmission line with a characteristic impedance ($Z_0$) typically rated at 120 ohms. When high-speed digital edges propagate down an unterminated serial cable, the signal hits the open-circuit cable end and reflects backward, interfering destructively with subsequent data bits. To prevent these reflections, 120-ohm metal film termination resistors must be installed across Lines A and B at the two extreme physical ends of the multi-drop trunk line. In addition, fail-safe biasing resistors (pull-up on Line B to 5V, pull-down on Line A to ground) are installed at the master to ensure that when all slave transceivers are tri-stated in high-impedance receive mode, the differential voltage remains stable at a defined idle state ($> +200\,\text{mV}$), preventing UART receivers from falsely triggering on floating electrical noise.

The timing constraints of the Modbus RTU frame delimiter are equally vital for protocol compliance. At standard industrial baud rates of 9600 bps or 19200 bps, the $t_{3.5}$ silent interval is directly proportional to character transmission time. However, for high-speed serial networks operating above 19200 bps (such as 38400, 57600, or 115200 bps), the Modbus specification establishes fixed, non-linear timing rules: $t_{3.5}$ is fixed at exactly 1.75 milliseconds, and the inter-character timeout $t_{1.5}$ is fixed at 750 microseconds. This standard concession was introduced because the microscopic character transmission times at 115200 bps (approximately 95 microseconds per character) would yield a $t_{3.5}$ window of only 334 microseconds—a duration too short for standard industrial PLC microcontrollers to reliably service without experiencing false timeout interrupts due to operating system scheduling jitter.

parts.title: Day 51 Part 2 — CRC-16 Calculation & Error Detection (Modbus Polynomial 0xA001)
say: In high-interference industrial environments, physical RS-485 cables often run parallel to high-power conduits, servo drives, and switching converters. Consequently, transient voltage spikes can flip individual bits during transmission. To protect against undetected data corruption, every Modbus RTU frame terminates with a 16-bit Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC-16). Unlike simple additive checksums—which can be fooled by compensating byte errors—CRC-16 provides robust mathematical error detection, detecting 100% of single-bit and double-bit errors, 100% of burst errors up to 16 bits in length, and 99.998% of longer burst errors.

The Modbus specification mandates a specific CRC variant based on the generator polynomial $x^{16} + x^{15} + x^2 + 1$ (standard CRC-16-IBM). However, in Modbus RTU, the calculation is executed in bit-reversed (reflected) order, utilizing the reversed polynomial constant `0xA001` (the reflection of `0x8005`). The calculation algorithm initializes a 16-bit register to `0xFFFF`. For each byte of the message (excluding the CRC itself), the byte is XORed into the low byte of the CRC register. The register is then shifted right by one bit eight successive times. If the bit shifted out of the least significant bit (LSB) is a 1, the register is XORed with polynomial `0xA001`; if the bit is 0, no XOR is performed.

A critical protocol nuance that frequently traps firmware engineers is byte endianness. While Modbus 16-bit register addresses and register values are encoded in Big-Endian (most significant byte first), the trailing CRC-16 field is transmitted in Little-Endian order: the least significant byte (low byte) of the CRC is transmitted first, followed by the most significant byte (high byte). Failing to reverse the two CRC bytes will cause receiving slaves to reject every single transmission as corrupt.

In our hands-on implementation, we construct the `ModbusCrc16` engine. We implement the bit-reversal polynomial reduction algorithm, append valid little-endian CRC bytes to outgoing PDUs, and build a deterministic frame verification method.

The mathematical elegance of the Modbus RTU CRC-16 calculation lies in its hardware-oriented bit-reversed shift register architecture. In classical digital communications, Cyclic Redundancy Checks are implemented using polynomial division over Galois Field GF(2). Standard CRC-16-IBM utilizes the generator polynomial $x^{16} + x^{15} + x^2 + 1$, corresponding to the 16-bit binary value `0x8005`. However, in standard UART serial communications, data bytes are physically shifted out onto the wire least-significant bit (LSB) first. If standard polynomial division were applied, embedded microcontrollers would be forced to execute costly bit-reversal operations on every incoming and outgoing byte. To eliminate this CPU processing overhead, the designers of Modbus RTU inverted the polynomial, reflecting `0x8005` into `0xA001`, allowing the division algorithm to process data bits naturally in LSB-first order.

The calculation routine initializes an internal 16-bit accumulator to `0xFFFF`. Initializing the register to all ones rather than zero is a critical engineering requirement: if an uninitialized CRC register started at `0x0000`, a corrupted serial cable that emitted leading zero bytes would produce a resultant CRC of zero, allowing truncated or spurious zero-padded frames to pass through undetected. By presetting the register to `0xFFFF`, every leading zero byte alters the internal accumulator state immediately. During calculation, each incoming byte is XORed with the lower 8 bits of the accumulator, and the register is shifted right by one bit across eight iterations. If the bit shifted out of the least significant bit position is a 1, the accumulator is XORed with polynomial `0xA001`; if the bit is 0, the shift continues without XOR.

Endianness handling during final frame transmission is the single most frequent source of integration failures in industrial automation. While 16-bit Modbus data fields (such as starting register addresses and quantity counts) are transmitted in Big-Endian order (most significant byte first), the Modbus standard explicitly specifies that the 16-bit CRC must be transmitted in Little-Endian order: the least significant byte (low byte) is transmitted first, followed immediately by the most significant byte (high byte). Industrial edge gateways and protocol analyzers must adhere strictly to this byte reversal rule; transposing the CRC bytes will cause downstream PLCs to drop the frame silently, triggering timeout alarms in the master SCADA system.

parts.title: Day 51 Part 3 — Modbus Register Model & Function Codes (01, 02, 03, 04, 05, 06, 15, 16)
say: To interact with physical industrial processes, Modbus abstracts all device telemetry and control points into four distinct data tables. Understanding these four tables is essential for any industrial IoT engineer: First, Discrete Inputs (addresses 10001–19999) are read-only binary boolean values, typically representing physical digital sensors such as limit switches, proximity detectors, or interlock relays. Second, Coils (addresses 00001–09999) are read-write boolean values, representing controllable digital outputs such as solenoid valves, motor contactors, or warning lights.

Third, Input Registers (addresses 30001–39999) are read-only 16-bit word values, representing analog sensor measurements such as temperature from a thermocouple, pressure from a 4–20 mA transducer, or current from a CT meter. Fourth, Holding Registers (addresses 40001–49999) are read-write 16-bit word values, used for configuration parameters, setpoints, PID loop tuning constants, and multi-word data structures (such as 32-bit floating-point numbers or 64-bit energy counters).

Operations on these tables are governed by standardized Function Codes. The most widely used function codes include: Function 01 (Read Coils), Function 02 (Read Discrete Inputs), Function 03 (Read Holding Registers), Function 04 (Read Input Registers), Function 05 (Write Single Coil), Function 06 (Write Single Register), Function 15 (Write Multiple Coils), and Function 16 (Write Multiple Registers). When an invalid address or unsupported operation is requested, the slave does not return normal data; instead, it sets the most significant bit of the function code (e.g., Function 03 becomes Exception 0x83) and returns a 1-byte Exception Code (0x01 Illegal Function, 0x02 Illegal Data Address, 0x03 Illegal Data Value, or 0x04 Slave Device Failure).

In our hands-on implementation, we construct the `ModbusSlaveDevice`. We model the four internal memory tables, implement execution handlers for Function 03 (Read Holding), Function 06 (Write Single), and Function 16 (Write Multiple), and enforce Modbus exception handling.

To interact meaningfully with industrial automation hardware, engineers must master the relationship between Modbus register models and the physical I/O architecture of programmable logic controllers. In a typical manufacturing cell or water treatment facility, physical field sensors wire directly into PLC I/O expansion racks. Discrete Inputs (addresses 10001–19999) wire to binary dry contacts, optical interlocks, and emergency stop pushbuttons; because they reflect physical real-world states, they are strictly read-only and cannot be overridden by software commands. Conversely, Coils (addresses 00001–09999) wire to relay output cards that actuate solenoids, contactor coils, and indicator beacons; they are fully read-write, allowing supervisory SCADA platforms to command machinery states directly.

Analog signals are similarly segregated into Input Registers (addresses 30001–39999) and Holding Registers (addresses 40001–49999). Input registers capture measurements from 4–20 mA current loops, RTD temperature probes, and 0–10V pressure transducers, serving as read-only telemetry. Holding registers, by contrast, store operational setpoints, PID controller proportional-integral-derivative gains, and recipe parameters. Furthermore, because Modbus registers are strictly 16-bit unsigned words, modern industrial instruments encode higher-precision data types—such as IEEE 754 32-bit single-precision floating-point numbers or 64-bit energy totals—across two or four consecutive holding registers. Industrial software must account for manufacturer-specific word endianness, configuring byte swaps (e.g., Big-Endian vs Little-Endian Word Swap) to prevent corrupt readings.

When a Modbus master transmits a malformed or unauthorized command, the slave device must communicate the operational failure unambiguously without hanging the serial bus. Modbus achieves this through standardized Exception Responses. In an exception response, the slave echoes the requested function code with its most significant bit set (computed by adding `0x80` to the function code; for instance, Function 0x03 becomes 0x83). The payload consists of a single 1-byte Exception Code: 0x01 indicates that the requested function code is unsupported; 0x02 indicates that the target register address does not exist in the slave's memory table; 0x03 indicates that the value field contains invalid data; and 0x04 indicates that an unrecoverable internal hardware fault occurred during command execution. Robust master software inspects these exception codes to trigger actionable diagnostic alerts for plant technicians.

parts.title: Day 51 Part 4 — Modbus TCP Protocol: MBAP Header, Transaction IDs & Socket Multiplexing
say: As industrial facilities modernized in the late 1990s, plant architectures transitioned from slow, multi-drop RS-485 serial buses to high-speed Industrial Ethernet backbones. To bring Modbus onto Ethernet networks without breaking compatibility with existing PLC memory models, Schneider Electric created Modbus TCP (RFC 793 / IEC 61158). Modbus TCP operates over TCP/IP, listening on designated TCP port 502.

Modbus TCP introduces two fundamental architectural changes compared to Modbus RTU: First, because Ethernet and TCP provide built-in checksum and frame integrity verification (Ethernet CRC-32 and TCP 16-bit checksums), the serial CRC-16 is completely eliminated from Modbus TCP packets. Second, because TCP is a stream-oriented protocol that does not support inter-character timing gaps, the 3.5 character silent interval is replaced by a 7-byte Modbus Application Protocol (MBAP) header prepended to every request and response.

The MBAP header consists of four fields: Transaction Identifier (2 bytes, assigned by the client to pair asynchronous requests with responses), Protocol Identifier (2 bytes, always 0x0000 for Modbus), Length field (2 bytes, indicating the remaining byte count of the message including the Unit ID and PDU), and Unit Identifier (1 byte, corresponding to the legacy slave address, used when bridging to downstream RS-485 serial sub-networks). Because TCP provides connection-oriented streaming and Transaction IDs allow client multiplexing, a single Modbus TCP master can query dozens of industrial slaves concurrently across a single persistent TCP socket connection.

In our hands-on implementation, we construct the `ModbusTcpEngine`. We build the 7-byte MBAP header for outgoing industrial requests, increment monotonic transaction identifiers, parse incoming multi-word register responses, and extract telemetry payloads.

The transition from serial Modbus RTU to Modbus TCP represents a monumental leap in industrial networking bandwidth, scalability, and network architecture. Developed to run over standard IEEE 802.3 Ethernet and TCP/IP, Modbus TCP operates as a client-server protocol listening on IANA-assigned TCP port 502. By migrating to Ethernet, industrial facilities eliminated the severe physical constraints of RS-485—replacing 1200-meter distance limits, 32-device multi-drop ceilings, and 9600 bps baud rates with Gigabit fiber-optic backbones, managed industrial switches, and sub-millisecond packet delivery across enterprise LANs.

The core architectural innovation of Modbus TCP is the Modbus Application Protocol (MBAP) header. Because Ethernet provides robust link-layer error detection via 32-bit Frame Check Sequences (FCS) and TCP provides 16-bit transport-layer checksums, the serial CRC-16 is completely omitted from Modbus TCP frames. In its place, every message begins with a 7-byte MBAP header consisting of four distinct fields: The Transaction Identifier (2 bytes) is a unique sequence number assigned by the client to pair asynchronous requests with incoming responses across multiplexed TCP sockets; the Protocol Identifier (2 bytes) is permanently set to `0x0000`, identifying the payload as Modbus; the Length field (2 bytes) specifies the remaining byte count of the frame (including the Unit ID and PDU); and the Unit Identifier (1 byte) preserves legacy slave addressing, serving as a sub-network routing address when communicating with downstream RS-485 serial clusters through an Ethernet-to-serial gateway.

Socket lifecycle and connection management are critical operational concerns in enterprise Modbus TCP deployments. Constrained industrial hardware—such as micro-PLCs or digital power meters equipped with low-cost embedded Ethernet controllers—often have limited RAM, supporting only 4 to 8 concurrent TCP socket connections. If a SCADA system or IoT cloud polling service creates a new TCP connection for every polling transaction and tears it down immediately, the slave device's TCP stack quickly becomes exhausted with sockets stuck in `TIME_WAIT` state, leading to dropped connections and intermittent communication timeouts. Production-grade industrial IoT gateways prevent this socket starvation by maintaining long-lived persistent TCP connection pools, multiplexing dozens of asynchronous transactions across dedicated sockets with active keep-alive probes.
parts.code:
# Modbus TCP Protocol Engine & MBAP Header Formatter (RFC 793 / Modbus TCP)
class ModbusTcpEngine:
    def __init__(self):
        self.transaction_id_counter = 1

    def build_mbap_request(self, unit_id, function_code, address, quantity):
        # MBAP Header:
        # Transaction ID (2B), Protocol ID (2B = 0), Length (2B = Remaining bytes), Unit ID (1B)
        tid = self.transaction_id_counter
        self.transaction_id_counter += 1
        
        pdu = bytes([function_code]) + address.to_bytes(2, "big") + quantity.to_bytes(2, "big")
        length = len(pdu) + 1 # +1 for unit_id

        mbap = tid.to_bytes(2, "big") + bytes([0x00, 0x00]) + length.to_bytes(2, "big") + bytes([unit_id])
        return mbap + pdu

    def parse_mbap_response(self, raw_bytes):
        if len(raw_bytes) < 7:
            raise ValueError("Frame smaller than 7-byte MBAP header")
        
        tid = int.from_bytes(raw_bytes[0:2], "big")
        proto_id = int.from_bytes(raw_bytes[2:4], "big")
        length = int.from_bytes(raw_bytes[4:6], "big")
        unit_id = raw_bytes[6]
        pdu = raw_bytes[7:]

        return {
            "transaction_id": tid,
            "protocol_id": proto_id,
            "length": length,
            "unit_id": unit_id,
            "pdu_len": len(pdu),
            "pdu_hex": pdu.hex().upper()
        }

tcp_engine = ModbusTcpEngine()
req_bytes = tcp_engine.build_mbap_request(unit_id=1, function_code=0x04, address=0x0014, quantity=4)
# Emulate slave response: TID 1, Proto 0, Len 11 (Unit + Func + ByteCount + 4*2 bytes)
resp_pdu = bytes([0x04, 0x08, 0x01, 0x20, 0x02, 0x40, 0x03, 0x60, 0x04, 0x80])
resp_bytes = bytes([0x00, 0x01, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x0B, 0x01]) + resp_pdu

parsed_resp = tcp_engine.parse_mbap_response(resp_bytes)

print(f"Modbus TCP Request Hex: {req_bytes.hex().upper()} (Len={len(req_bytes)}B)")
print(f"MBAP Header: TID={parsed_resp['transaction_id']} Proto={parsed_resp['protocol_id']} Unit={parsed_resp['unit_id']}")
print(f"Parsed Response PDU: {parsed_resp['pdu_hex']} ({parsed_resp['pdu_len']} bytes)")

parts.title: Day 51 Part 5 — Masterclass Synthesis: Comprehensive Modbus RTU/TCP Industrial Bridge
say: We now bring together all the components of Day 51 into a production-grade masterclass simulation: the `ModbusIndustrialBridgeEngine`. In modern smart manufacturing and industrial IoT deployments, the biggest brownfield integration challenge is protocol bridging: converting legacy RS-485 serial Modbus RTU field devices into high-speed Modbus TCP or MQTT cloud telemetry streams without replacing expensive operational PLCs, meters, or machinery.

The `ModbusIndustrialBridgeEngine` acts as an edge gateway. On the OT side, it connects to an RS-485 serial bus, managing periodic polling tasks for multiple downstream slave units (e.g., Unit 1 for a pumping station, Unit 2 for a variable frequency drive). It calculates exact $t_{3.5}$ silent intervals, appends verified CRC-16 checksums, and handles timeout retries. On the IT side, the engine wraps the retrieved register values into Modbus TCP MBAP framing and prepares the data for enterprise SCADA ingestion or cloud time-series dashboards.

Furthermore, the engine maintains real-time operational telemetry across all polling cycles. It monitors poll success rates, tracks CRC corruption anomalies (which alert plant engineers to physical wiring degradation or electromagnetic interference), logs exception codes, and buffers readings in a high-speed telemetry cache for edge analytics.

Upon executing a complete multi-task polling cycle and verifying end-to-end data conversion across both serial RTU and Ethernet TCP formats, the engine latches and emits our verified certification token: `MODBUS_INDUSTRIAL_PROTOCOL_ENGINE_GRADE_A_PLUS_CERTIFIED`. This marks your mastery of fundamental industrial operational technology protocols.

In modern operational technology environments, the industrial edge gateway serves as the vital translation bridge uniting legacy fieldbus networks with enterprise IT and cloud analytics platforms. An industrial gateway deployed on a factory floor connects simultaneously to physical RS-485 multi-drop serial trunks and enterprise Industrial Ethernet switches. The gateway's core software orchestrates continuous polling engines: it cycles through configured register maps across dozens of slave PLCs, pacing serial requests with precise $t_{3.5}$ idle intervals, verifying received CRC-16 checksums, and buffering the retrieved operational parameters into high-speed in-memory telemetry caches.

On the northbound IT side, the gateway translates this raw binary register telemetry into standardized industrial data streams. Rather than requiring cloud applications to understand arcane 16-bit Modbus memory offsets, the gateway encapsulates register values into structured, self-describing JSON or binary formats—such as OPC UA nodes or MQTT Sparkplug B topic namespaces. For example, Holding Registers 40010 and 40011 are automatically decoded as a 32-bit floating-point value, annotated with engineering units (e.g., 'MainPump_FlowRate_GPM: 142.5'), and published to an enterprise message broker with microsecond-accurate time stamps.

Furthermore, edge gateways implement intelligent store-and-forward buffering to survive WAN outages. In remote facilities such as oil and gas wellheads, municipal water pumping stations, or solar generation farms, the cellular or satellite uplink backhaul to the cloud can drop intermittently. During communication blackouts, the gateway does not discard polled Modbus readings; it stages telemetry in an embedded SQLite database or circular ring buffer on local flash memory. Once WAN connectivity is restored, the gateway securely transmits the historical backlog in chronological order without overloading the upstream telemetry broker.

In addition, cybersecurity hardening on the industrial gateway is critical because legacy Modbus protocols lack native encryption or authentication. Modern industrial edge architectures wrap unencrypted Modbus TCP payloads inside encrypted WireGuard VPN tunnels, IPsec links, or Transport Layer Security (TLS 1.3) sessions, preventing unauthorized packet injection or eavesdropping across plant-to-cloud boundaries.

Finally, enterprise production verification demands continuous telemetry observability and automated fault detection. The `ModbusIndustrialBridgeEngine` continuously tracks communication health metrics: total polls executed, successful TCP relays, CRC checksum corruptions, and exception occurrences. A sudden spike in CRC errors immediately flags physical layer issues—such as a loose RS-485 screw terminal, missing termination resistors, or failing cable shielding—empowering plant maintenance personnel to remediate issues before critical machinery trips. By executing full polling cycles and satisfying all Grade A+ verification invariants, the engine latches our verified certification token: `MODBUS_INDUSTRIAL_PROTOCOL_ENGINE_GRADE_A_PLUS_CERTIFIED`.

options: It polls legacy RS-485 serial slaves using Modbus RTU and bridges the register telemetry into high-speed Modbus TCP or cloud streams.
